clue.text: Where everything in the garden is lovely

definitions.text: Where everything in the garden is lovely

parts.words: Where everything in the garden is lovely
parts.note: surface reading: a literal spot in a pretty, well-kept garden

parts.words: everything in the garden is lovely
parts.note: setter's reading: the idiom for a situation where all is going well, a life of ease

explanation.surface: A gardener admires the one patch where every plant is thriving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everything in the garden is lovely' is a stock phrase meaning all is well, and the answer is the idiom for that easy, comfortable state, which literally is a flower patch.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a situation of comfort and luxury, which is exactly what the garden saying expresses figuratively.

clue.text: Will Abraham be such a friend in the hereafter?

definitions.text: Will Abraham be such a friend in the hereafter?

parts.note: surface reading: a very close companion, a dear pal
setter's reading: Abraham's resting place for the righteous dead in the Gospel parable of Lazarus

explanation.surface: Wondering whether the patriarch will be a close companion in heaven.
explanation.walkthrough: A close pal is a '___ friend', and in Luke's Gospel the dead Lazarus is carried to 'Abraham's ___', meaning heaven.
explanation.definitionFit: The chest, figuratively the place of closeness and comfort, gives both the intimate-friend idiom and the biblical image of paradise.

clue.text: Grace seldom associated with this food

definitions.text: Grace seldom associated with this food

parts.note: surface reading: a prayer said before eating a meal
setter's reading: W. G. Grace, the great Victorian cricketer, who rarely scored nought

explanation.surface: A remark that people rarely say a prayer before eating a certain dish.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a score of zero is a duck, and the scoreboard zero is likened to an egg; W. G. Grace was a famously prolific English batsman.
explanation.definitionFit: The score of nothing at cricket is named for the egg shape of the zero, so it is literally a food.

clue.text: The man has whisky, being one of us

parts.note: a fellow is a man or chap
'the creature' is old Irish slang for whiskey

explanation.surface: A man with a glass of Scotch, a regular person like the rest of us.
explanation.definitionFit: Another human being who shares our nature is a companion in the species, someone like ourselves.

clue.text: Driving out for a pleasure trip round the south

indicators.note: going round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses the other

parts.note: an excursion for fun
abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: Motoring out on a leisurely excursion around the southern counties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driving out' looks like part of the motoring scene but means expelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Expelling or forcing someone from a position is the same as removing them by force.

clue.text: Unusual sea bird, possibly Chinese?

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A strange seabird that might have flown in from China.
explanation.definitionFit: Something from Asia, such as China, belongs to the Orient, the part of the world toward sunrise.

clue.text: Downright monotonous

definitions.meaning: first meaning: absolute, as in a refusal that is complete and blunt
second meaning: dull and lacking variation in tone

explanation.walkthrough: The two words read like one phrase describing something utterly dull, but each is a separate meaning of the same short word.
explanation.definitionFit: A blunt refusal is called this, and a voice lacking any lively variation is described the same way.

clue.text: Drunk, the man's supple .

parts.note: lit is slang for intoxicated
the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: A drunk man becomes surprisingly loose-limbed.
explanation.definitionFit: A flexible, graceful body that bends easily is described by both words.

clue.text: Compositions and agreements about Old Bob

indicators.note: lying about something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps around another

parts.note: formal agreements between nations
a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s

explanation.surface: Pieces of writing and pacts concerning a man called Bob.
explanation.walkthrough: Bob is British slang for a shilling, a coin abolished in 1971, whose symbol was s.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal written essays or dissertations on a subject are pieces of writing, i.e. literary works.

clue.text: One who runs the Beauty page?

definitions.text: One who runs the Beauty page?

parts.note: surface reading: the cosmetics and grooming section of a newspaper
setter's reading: beauty lies in the face, so the person in charge of facial parts

explanation.surface: Who is in charge of the newspaper's make-up and grooming section?
explanation.walkthrough: The face's parts, eyes, nose and mouth, share a name with a newspaper's magazine-style articles, and beauty is a matter of good ones.
explanation.definitionFit: The journalist responsible for long non-news articles in a paper would naturally oversee a lifestyle beauty section.

clue.text: Disgusted the French-cutters

parts.note: sick of something means disgusted by it
the plural form of 'the' in French

explanation.surface: A complaint that the French reapers were revolted by something.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'French-cutters' is surface glue; the definition is just the last word.
explanation.definitionFit: These curved blades are tools for cutting grain or grass, hence plural cutting implements.

clue.text: Put up with cover-point

parts.note: a sheath is a protective covering, as for a blade
a point of the compass, east

explanation.surface: A cricketer grudgingly tolerating the cover-point fielding position.
explanation.walkthrough: Cover-point is a fielding position in cricket, but here the hyphenated term splits into two pieces. To put up a sword is to return it to its scabbard.
explanation.definitionFit: Putting up a sword means returning it into its scabbard, which is exactly what this verb describes.

clue.text: Capitalist voice must change (to suit him?)

indicators.note: a change rearranges what was there before, so these letters get reordered

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A capitalist's opinions must shift to fit his own interests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capitalist' looks like a money-maker, but it means a dweller in a capital city, here Moscow. The bracketed aside makes the whole clue a wry political joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of Moscow lives in the Russian capital city, so is jokingly a capital-ist.

clue.text: Doctor, it's a pleasure

definitions.meaning: first meaning, as a verb: to give medical care to
second meaning, as a noun: a delightful thing

explanation.surface: A patient politely telling the physician what a joy the visit is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' looks like a form of address but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A physician will give medical care to a patient, and a delightful indulgence is also called by this word.

clue.text: With uncanny skill, soldier prepared for rain

indicators.note: someone prepared for wet weather is wrapped inside a coat, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: the coat worn in rain, short for mackintosh
an American private soldier

explanation.surface: A deft soldier who was sensibly ready for a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: A mac (mackintosh) is a British raincoat; the soldier dressed for rain is inside one.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleight of hand and conjuring display a seemingly supernatural ability, which is what this word names.

clue.text: Reduces some trade difficulties

indicators.note: difficulties suggest trouble and disorder, so these letters are put into a different order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Easing certain commercial problems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some' looks like a hidden-word signal, but here it is part of the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To tone something down or lessen its intensity is to make it less extreme.

clue.text: Creates the New Look for teenagers

indicators.note: a new look is a fresh rearrangement, recalling Dior's restyling of fashion

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fashion designer launches a fresh style aimed at young people.
explanation.walkthrough: The New Look was Christian Dior's famous 1947 fashion line, which makes the surface about clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To produce or bring something into existence is the shared meaning of both verbs.

clue.text: Orange agent, worried about Ireland

indicators.note: worried means agitated and shaken about, so these letters are jumbled
being about something means around it, so the jumbled piece encloses the other

parts.note: the letters rearranged
the poetic name for Ireland

explanation.surface: An Orange Order operative anxious over Irish affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes the Orange Order, Protestant loyalists in Northern Ireland, but the answer is a citrus fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: A small, loose-skinned mandarin type is a kind of citrus fruit, hence an example of the fruit named.

clue.text: Ended split (about time!) and cleared off

indicators.note: a word that is split open has room for something else placed in the gap

parts.note: ended, in the sense of came to a stop
a spell is a period of time

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that a long relationship has finally broken up.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan's 'Sended' is a misreading of 'Ended'. 'about' tells you the split word goes around the period of time.
explanation.definitionFit: To drive away doubts or fears, making them vanish, is to have removed them entirely.

clue.text: He got burnt lighting a candle

definitions.text: He got burnt lighting a candle

parts.words: He got burnt lighting a candle
parts.note: surface reading: someone scorched his fingers with a match
setter's reading: the Protestant bishop burnt at Oxford in 1555, who said they would that day light such a candle in England as would never be put out

explanation.surface: A careless man singes himself while lighting a candle.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Latimer, burnt at the stake with Ridley, famously told his fellow martyr 'we shall this day light such a candle'.
explanation.definitionFit: The English reforming bishop martyred by fire spoke the famous words about kindling an undying flame of faith.

clue.text: Gets urges about early start

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: drives are strong urges or instincts

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter only

parts.note: the opening letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone acquires the impulse to get going early.
explanation.definitionFit: To obtain or draw something from a source is to receive it.

clue.text: Invests in flags

definitions.meaning: first meaning: puts money into something, as in pouring cash into a venture
second meaning: droops or declines in strength

explanation.surface: Someone putting money into bunting or banners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flags' looks like a noun for banners, but it is a verb meaning weakens.
explanation.definitionFit: One pours capital into a business, and a tiring person gradually droops; both senses share this verb.

clue.text: How some contrive to hold our attention

indicators.note: taking only some of the following words means the letters lie within them

parts.note: the letters run across the join of the two words

explanation.surface: A remark on how certain performers manage to keep an audience gripped.
explanation.definitionFit: A gripping show fixes the audience's gaze firmly, the way a metal pin fixes plates together.

clue.text: Contends about wickets — hence scenes

indicators.note: being about something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: competes or strives
the cricket scorecard abbreviation for wickets

explanation.surface: A bowler competing over wickets, producing dramatic moments on the field.
explanation.definitionFit: Landscapes or vistas seen from a spot are prospects, the sights before one's eyes.

clue.text: Hard-won affection of business men

parts.note: surface reading: love or fondness that took effort to earn
setter's reading: affection in its old sense of an ailment, the condition busy workers earn through hard toil

explanation.surface: Executives finally winning someone's love after much effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Affection' here is the medical sense, a bodily condition, and the hard work that wins it is the working day itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Weariness is a bodily state that comes from long labour, so overworked executives acquire it.

clue.text: Of which the bridge is not as big as it sounds

definitions.text: Of which the bridge is not as big as it sounds

parts.note: surface reading: some bridge that seems grander than it really is

parts.words: not as big as it sounds
parts.note: setter's reading: the small Venetian bridge whose name sounds like a word for bigness

explanation.surface: A remark about a bridge whose reputation exceeds its actual dimensions.
explanation.walkthrough: Venice's Bridge of Sighs is quite small, though its name said out loud sounds like 'size'.
explanation.definitionFit: Long audible breaths of sorrow give the famous Venetian bridge its name, from prisoners crossing it.

clue.text: The more abstruse kind of proposition

indicators.note: abstruse means obscure and hard to follow, so these letters are muddled up

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumble that the more obscure a statement is, the more it is valued.
explanation.definitionFit: In mathematics, a statement proved from axioms is a particular type of logical assertion.

clue.text: Perhaps given to putting up the bans?

definitions.text: Perhaps given to putting up the bans?

parts.note: surface reading: posting the banns, the church notice that a couple will marry
setter's reading: proposing prohibitions, forbidding things outright

explanation.surface: Someone inclined to announce forthcoming weddings in church.
explanation.walkthrough: Banns are the notices read in church before a wedding; 'bans' sounds the same but means prohibitions.
explanation.definitionFit: Forbidding a proposal by official refusal is the act of putting up prohibitions.

clue.text: Billy, wearing a nice new one, fell in the fire

definitions.text: Billy, wearing a nice new one, fell in the fire

parts.words: Billy, wearing a nice new one
parts.note: surface reading: a boy called Billy in a new outfit has an accident

parts.words: Billy, wearing a nice new one
parts.note: setter's reading: King Billy, William of Orange, whose followers march wearing an orange band over the shoulder

explanation.surface: A child in brand-new clothes tumbles into the fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: King Billy is William of Orange, and Orangemen march in a sash; how 'fell in the fire' fits is unclear from this copy, which may be garbled.
explanation.definitionFit: A decorative band worn across the body is what an Orange marcher wears in honour of King William.

clue.text: Mothballs, perhaps, betray prior to acolytes

parts.note: the prefix meaning before
acolytes assist the priest at the altar as servers

explanation.surface: Little balls in the wardrobe somehow giving away the altar boys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'betray' does no work in the wordplay and is probably a garbled word in this copy; the answer is just the prefix plus the altar helpers.
explanation.definitionFit: Mothballs keep clothes safe from insects, so they are an example of things that protect and keep.
